div.head: II Cn 19.2
div.ab: Gyf se þonne berste, nime þonne leafe ægþer ge heonan ge þanan, þæt he mote hentan æfter his agenan.
Gyf se þanne berste, nime þanne geleafe ge heonon ge þanon, þæt he mote hemtan æfter his ágenan.
Qui si fallat, tunc licentiam accipiat, ut abhinc et inde suum audeat perquirere.
And gyf se ðonne byrste, nime ðonne leafe ge heonan ge ðeonan þæt he mote hæntan æfter [h]is agan.
Gyf se þonne berste, nime þonne leafe ægþer ge heonon ge þanan þæt he mote hentan æfter his agenan.
And if this summons fails, he shall get leave, either from the one court or the other, to take his own measures for the recovery of his property.
And if this proves futile, he shall get permission either here or from the previous court to repossess his property.
And if this then fails, he is to get permission either from this court or that, that he may seize his own.
Wenn dieser aber fehlschlägt, dann nehme er Erlaubniss, dass er von hier und da [allerseits in Selbsthilfe] hinter seinem Eigenthum her zugreifen dürfe.
But if that fails, then let him take permission, from here and there [i.e. from both courts], to seize [in self-help] for his own property.
div.note: G's ‘ægþer’ is missing from the other MSS (compare Consiliatio ‘utrimque’). A's ‘hemtan’ for ‘hentan’.

literally, “hence or thence” which, judging by the order, seems to go with the permission (sic Miss Robertson), though Quadritpartitus and Liebermann take it in the next clause, where it would mean that the distraint might be made anywhere on the defaulter’s property.
